question: Why does Docker-in-Docker require privileged: true in GitLab Runner configuration?

options.text: This is a GitLab security requirement — without it the Runner won't start a service
options.explanation: The requirement comes not from GitLab, but from Docker itself. The Runner needs to pass extended kernel privileges to the container.

options.text: Without privileged, Docker cannot read Dockerfiles from the repository
options.explanation: Reading files from the repository does not require privileged. This is normal file access.

options.text: Privileged mode is only needed for pushing to Docker Registry
options.explanation: Pushing to a Registry is a normal network operation, does not require privileged. Privileges are needed to run the Docker daemon.

options.text: The Docker daemon inside a container needs access to the host kernel to manage namespaces and cgroups
options.explanation: Exactly. The Docker daemon manages kernel primitives (namespaces, cgroups, overlay FS). Without privileged, the container lacks these rights and the daemon won't start.

question: What is the main advantage of Kaniko over Docker-in-Docker?

options.text: Kaniko supports a wider set of Dockerfile instructions
options.explanation: Kaniko supports most Dockerfile instructions, but that is not its main advantage over dind.

options.text: Kaniko does not require privileged mode — builds happen in userspace without a Docker daemon
options.explanation: The key advantage. Kaniko reads the Dockerfile and builds layers in userspace, without requiring privileged access to the host kernel. This is critical for secure production environments.

options.text: Kaniko builds images faster because it doesn't need to start a daemon
options.explanation: Speed is not the main advantage. On first run, Kaniko can even be slower. The main point is security.

options.text: Kaniko does not require Docker Registry — images are stored locally on the Runner
options.explanation: This is wrong. Kaniko pushes images to a Registry — local storage is not its feature.

question: How does Kaniko cache layers between builds?

options.text: Kaniko does not support caching — it rebuilds all layers every time
options.explanation: Kaniko supports caching via the --cache and --cache-repo flags.

options.text: Kaniko stores layer cache in Docker Registry via --cache=true and --cache-repo flags
options.explanation: Correct. Kaniko pushes cached layers to a separate Registry repository (e.g., registry.example.com/project/cache). On the next build it downloads them from there.

options.text: Kaniko uses the GitLab cache mechanism via cache: paths in .gitlab-ci.yml
options.explanation: GitLab cache is a mechanism for files on disk. Kaniko has its own caching mechanism via Registry.

options.text: Cache is stored locally on the Runner in /var/lib/kaniko/cache
options.explanation: Kaniko does not use local cache on the Runner disk — this contradicts its daemonless architecture.

question:
Your Dockerfile has this structure:

FROM node:20 AS builder
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html

Why is this bad practice?

options.text: node_modules, .git and .env can end up in the builder image and bloat it
options.explanation: Without .dockerignore, COPY . . copies node_modules (hundreds of MB), .git history, .env with secrets. The builder image becomes huge, and secrets can leak.

options.text: Any code change invalidates the npm ci layer cache, even if dependencies didn't change
options.explanation: COPY . . copies everything, including source code. If any .ts file changes — the COPY layer changes — the next RUN npm ci rebuilds from scratch, even though package.json was untouched.

options.text: Multi-stage build is not supported when using dind
options.explanation: Multi-stage build is a standard Docker feature, works with all build methods: dind, Kaniko, buildx.

options.text: FROM nginx:alpine cannot use --from=builder
options.explanation: COPY --from=builder is correct multi-stage build syntax. This is normal practice.

question: What does --cache-from $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:latest mean in a docker build command?

options.text: Docker downloads the latest image and uses its layers as cache when building the new image
options.explanation: Exactly. Docker compares Dockerfile instructions with the downloaded image layers. Matching layers are not rebuilt — they are taken from cache. This saves 80%+ of build time.

options.text: Docker will not publish the latest image, only use it for cache
options.explanation: This is only about cache during build. Publishing is handled separately by docker push.

options.text: latest will be overwritten by the new image at the end of the build
options.explanation: This is not related to --cache-from. Overwriting latest happens on docker push, not on build.

options.text: The build will fail if the latest image does not exist in the Registry
options.explanation: No. If the image is not found (docker pull returns an error), the build continues without cache. That's why || true is used after docker pull.

question: The DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR variable is set to an empty string in a dind job. What risk does this create?

options.text: Docker won't start without TLS certificates
options.explanation: Docker will start, but will listen on the unsecured port 2375 instead of 2376.

options.text: Any process or service in the container network can connect to the Docker daemon and control it without authentication
options.explanation: Without TLS, Docker listens on port 2375 without encryption or authentication. In a multi-container environment, this means any process can launch containers, read host files, etc.

options.text: Builds will be slower — without TLS there is no traffic compression
options.explanation: TLS does not affect compression speed. The risk is about security, not performance.

options.text: Images will not be saved to Registry due to missing certificates
options.explanation: Registry authentication and TLS for dind are different mechanisms. Without TLS for dind, pushing to Registry will work.

question: How to properly authenticate with GitLab Container Registry when using Kaniko?

options.text: Add docker login in before_script before running Kaniko
options.explanation: docker login does not work in the Kaniko container — there is no Docker CLI there. You need /kaniko/.docker/config.json.

options.text: Kaniko automatically uses $CI_JOB_TOKEN to access GitLab Registry
options.explanation: Kaniko has no built-in GitLab integration. You must explicitly provide credentials via config.json.

options.text: Create /kaniko/.docker/config.json with base64-encoded Registry credentials
options.explanation: Correct. Kaniko uses the standard Docker config.json for authentication. It needs to be created manually: printf '%s:%s' user password | base64 and written to /kaniko/.docker/config.json.

options.text: Pass CI_REGISTRY_USER and CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD as environment variables — Kaniko picks them up automatically
options.explanation: Kaniko does not read these variables automatically. You need to explicitly create config.json.

question: In a pipeline there is a job that runs tests inside a Docker image. The test job itself runs in dind. How to correctly pass test results from the container to GitLab?

options.text: Use docker run with host directory mount: -v $(pwd)/results:/app/results
options.explanation: Correct. Mount the CI job directory into the container. Tests write results to /app/results, which appear in $(pwd)/results on the job. Then this directory goes into artifacts.

options.text: Specify artifacts directly in docker run via the --artifact flag
options.explanation: There is no such flag in docker run. For file transfer, use volume mount or docker cp.

options.text: Tests inside docker run cannot transfer artifacts to GitLab
options.explanation: Results can be obtained — through volume mount or docker cp.

options.text: Use docker commit to save container changes
options.explanation: docker commit creates a new image from a container. This does not transfer files to GitLab artifacts.

question: A project uses GitHub Actions. You need to build a Docker image. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Docker is already installed on ubuntu-latest runner, dind is not needed. For optimization, use docker/setup-buildx-action
options.explanation: Exactly. GitHub-hosted runners (ubuntu-latest) already have Docker. setup-buildx-action enables BuildKit with extended caching capabilities (type=gha cache).

options.text: You need to set up dind like in GitLab — add privileged: true to the workflow
options.explanation: In GitHub Actions, Docker is available on ubuntu-latest runner by default. No need to separately configure dind or privileged mode.

options.text: In GitHub Actions you can only use Kaniko, not Docker
options.explanation: You can use either. Docker is preferred on GitHub Actions because it is already available without setup.

options.text: GitHub Actions does not support Docker image builds
options.explanation: It does, and very well. There are official actions: docker/build-push-action, docker/setup-buildx-action.

question: Why add || true after docker pull $IMAGE:latest in a build script?

options.text: So the pipeline doesn't fail on the first build when the latest image doesn't exist in Registry yet
options.explanation: Correct. docker pull exits with code 1 if the image is not found. On the first pipeline run, the latest image doesn't exist — without || true the entire job would fail because of this single command.

options.text: So GitLab doesn't count pull as an error on slow Registry
options.explanation: A slow Registry would cause a timeout, not a non-zero exit code. || true is needed for a different reason.

options.text: Docker pull returns an error on bad connection, || true makes the build resilient
options.explanation: This is partially true, but not the main reason. The primary case is the absence of the image on the first build.

options.text: || true is needed so subsequent commands can overwrite the pulled image
options.explanation: Subsequent docker build commands will create a new image regardless of the pull result. || true only ignores the error.

question: You notice that building a Docker image takes 8 minutes, even though only one TypeScript file changed. In the Dockerfile, instructions are arranged as: COPY . . -> RUN npm ci -> RUN npm run build. What needs to be fixed?

options.text: Reorder instructions: first COPY package*.json ./, then RUN npm ci, then COPY . .
options.explanation: The key fix. npm ci will only run when package*.json changes. Changing .ts files won't touch this layer.

options.text: Add .dockerignore, excluding node_modules, .git, coverage, dist
options.explanation: Also important. Without .dockerignore, COPY . . copies node_modules (hundreds of MB), which slows context transfer to the Docker daemon and invalidates cache.

options.text: Replace RUN npm ci with RUN npm install for faster installation
options.explanation: npm install does not solve the caching problem. npm ci is even preferable in CI — it is deterministic and faster with a lock file.

options.text: Enable DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 and use --cache-from the previous image
options.explanation: BuildKit and --cache-from complement Dockerfile optimization. BuildKit builds independent layers in parallel, --cache-from allows reusing layers between pipelines.

question: The team uses Kaniko with the --snapshot-mode=redo flag. What does this change?

options.text: Kaniko rebuilds all layers from scratch on every run, ignoring cache
options.explanation: redo does not mean a full rebuild. It is a mode for computing diffs between layers.

options.text: --snapshot-mode=redo is only needed for multi-stage builds
options.explanation: redo is useful for any Dockerfile. Images with many RUN commands benefit the most.

options.text: Kaniko saves filesystem snapshots to /tmp to speed up the next run
options.explanation: Kaniko snapshots are used during the current build to create image layers, but are not saved between runs.

options.text: A faster filesystem comparison algorithm: Kaniko executes commands and compares only changed files, instead of a full tree traversal
options.explanation: Correct. The redo mode is faster than the time mode (default), because it only recalculates files changed by the RUN command, rather than the entire tree. Recommended for most Dockerfiles.

question: You write a pipeline: a build image is assembled in dind, then a test job should run this image and execute smoke tests. How to pass the image between jobs?

options.text: Use cache: paths: [/var/lib/docker] to cache layers between jobs
options.explanation: Caching /var/lib/docker is not recommended — these are Docker daemon internal files that may be incorrect when restored. Use a Registry instead.

options.text: Use GitLab artifacts: save docker save output, load via docker load
options.explanation: A working approach for small images. docker save > image.tar -> artifacts -> docker load < image.tar. Downside: the tar file can be large.

options.text: Images are automatically shared between dind jobs on the same Runner
options.explanation: Each dind service is an isolated container with a separate daemon. Image layers are not automatically shared between jobs.

options.text: Push the image to GitLab Registry in the build job, pull it in the test job
options.explanation: The standard approach. Build pushes to Registry with a SHA tag, test does docker pull with the same tag. Reliable and scalable.

question: Under what conditions should you tag an image as latest?

options.text: Only when creating a git tag — latest should correspond to the last release
options.explanation: This is also a reasonable approach, but not the only one. Many teams use latest for main. For version tags they use separate image tags: v1.2.3.

options.text: Only when pushing to the main/master branch — latest should mean 'the last stable version'
options.explanation: The correct convention. latest is updated only for main, to mean 'what is currently in production'. Feature branches use their own tags (branch name or SHA).

options.text: On every successful pipeline run — latest should always point to the last successful build
options.explanation: If latest is updated on every commit (including feature branches), it loses meaning — you can't tell what exactly is deployed to production.

options.text: Never — latest is not recommended in production pipelines
options.explanation: latest is convenient as a human-readable tag for the main branch. The problem is not latest itself, but its misuse (overwriting on every commit from any branch).

question: What is the difference between --target builder and a normal docker build without --target in a multi-stage Dockerfile?

options.text: --target is only needed when using Kaniko — standard docker build ignores this flag
options.explanation: --target is a standard docker build flag, works with all tools: docker CLI, buildx, Kaniko, and others.

options.text: --target builder builds only the first stage and stops, ignoring the production stage
options.explanation: Correct. docker build --target builder stops after the stage named builder. This is useful for running tests in the build environment without assembling the full production image.

options.text: No difference — Docker always builds all stages
options.explanation: With --target, Docker stops at the specified stage and does not execute subsequent ones. This is the key difference.

options.text: --target builder is always faster because it builds fewer layers
options.explanation: This is true for this example, but not always. --target can point to a later stage that requires all previous ones.
